2, 2014 , work injury. The Hospital co ntends the ALJ erred by interpreting the 
independent medical examiner’s (IME’S) opinion to contain an “unambiguous” 
assessment of no work capacity , and by adopting that interpretation .  We disagree 
and affirm the decision.

both victims. Fernandez's alleged co-conspirator, Patrick Darge, testi-

der for hire and a frearms offense, and the District Court imposed two 
consecutive life sentences. 
Fernandez pursued multiple avenues of relief. He frst asked the Dis-

that they did not contain relevant information, though the judge noted 
he was “troubled” by the Government's lenient treatment of Rivera. 
The Second Circuit affrmed the conviction and sentence, rejecting both 
the Brady claim and Fernandez's insuffciency-of-evidence argument.

PITCHFORD v. CAIN 
certiorari to the united states court of appeals for 
the fth circuit 
No. 24–7351. Argued March 31, 2026—Decided May 28, 2026 
In 2004, two black teenagers, Terry Pitchford and Eric Bullins, robbed a 
grocery store near Grenada, Mississippi. During the robbery, Bullins 
shot and killed the white store owner. Bullins reached a plea agree-
ment and received a 20-year sentence for the homicide. The State 
charged Pitchford with capital murder and sought the death penalty. 
During jury selection at Pitchford's trial, the prosecutor used peremp-
tory strikes against four of the fve black potential jurors. As this 
Court held in Batson v. Kentucky, 476 U. S. 79, the Equal Protection 
Clause bars prosecutors from exercising peremptory challenges based 
on race. In Batson and subsequent cases, the Court has spelled out a 
three-step process for a trial court to determine whether a prosecutor 
employed a peremptory challenge based on race. Here, Pitchford's 
counsel raised an objection under Batson and made a prima facie show-
ing that the strikes of the four black jurors were based on race (step 
one). The trial court asked the prosecutor for race-neutral reasons for

items.title: Federal judge blocks attempts to restrict mail-in voting
items.content_text:
AUGUSTA, MAINE
– A federal judge in Boston blocked the Trump administration from interfering with states’ rights to conduct mail-in voting for the upcoming November elections, now 67 days away. Judge Indira Talwani ruled yesterday that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed in proving the administration’s order was unconstitutional.
“Last night’s decision was wonderful news for Maine voters who rely on absentee voting,”
Secretary Bellows said
. “The judge made clear that the states, not the federal government, are in charge of elections. That goes to the heart of our legal fights in court against the Trump Administration. We will continue to stand with other states and voting rights advocates across the nation to defend the voting rights – including the right to vote by mail – for every citizen.”
In the decision, Judge Talwani wrote, “the Constitution charges the States with election administration” going on to say that no law has been passed by Congress that “would permit the USPS to regulate election mail.” The judge went even further to note that with just two months to the election, it would an expensive and likely impossible task for the 2026 election, saying, “Plaintiff States face irreparable harm where they are required to comply with a likely unconstitutional regulation for which compliance is practically impossible.”
###
Attachment:
read the 08-27-26 order
